subject: Isaac Newton
overview: Isaac Newton was an English mathematician and physicist, a farmer's son from Lincolnshire who became a Cambridge professor and worked out the laws of motion and universal gravitation. His book the Principia showed that the same force pulling an apple to the ground keeps the Moon in orbit, and he also invented a form of calculus, split white light into colours with prisms and built the first practical reflecting telescope. Later in life he moved to London, where he ran the Royal Mint and presided over the Royal Society.

key_moments.title: Plague years at Woolsthorpe
key_moments.text: When the **Great Plague** closed the University of Cambridge, the young graduate went home to his family farm at **Woolsthorpe** in Lincolnshire. Working alone, he laid the groundwork of his **calculus**, ran experiments on light and began thinking about gravity, a burst of work later called his annus mirabilis, or year of wonders. Decades afterwards, an old Newton told his friend **William Stukeley** that the idea of gravitation had come to him there while watching an apple fall, the origin of the apple story still told today.
claims: The University of Cambridge closed in 1665 because of the Great Plague.
Isaac Newton returned to Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire while the University of Cambridge was closed.
Isaac Newton developed early ideas on calculus, optics and gravitation during the plague years of 1665 and 1666.
William Stukeley recorded that Isaac Newton linked the idea of gravitation to watching an apple fall.

key_moments.title: A new telescope and a theory of colour
key_moments.text: Newton built a small **reflecting telescope** that used a curved mirror instead of a lens, which avoided the coloured fringes that spoiled the images of ordinary refracting telescopes. Its success with the **Royal Society** got him elected a Fellow in 1672, and that year he published his theory that **white light is a mixture of colours**, shown by splitting sunlight with a prism. The paper drew sharp criticism from **Robert Hooke**, and the quarrel left Newton so bitter that he long avoided publishing at all.
claims: Isaac Newton built a reflecting telescope in 1668.
Isaac Newton was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1672.
Isaac Newton argued that white light is made up of a spectrum of colours, using experiments with prisms.
Robert Hooke criticised Isaac Newton's theory of light.

key_moments.title: Halley's question and the Principia
key_moments.text: In 1684 the astronomer **Edmond Halley** visited Cambridge and asked what path a planet would follow if pulled toward the Sun by a force weakening with the square of distance. Newton answered at once that it would be an ellipse, and Halley's prodding turned that answer into the **Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica**, published in 1687, which set out the **three laws of motion** and **universal gravitation**. The Royal Society had spent its budget on a lavish book about fish, so **Halley paid for the printing himself**.
claims: Edmond Halley visited Isaac Newton in Cambridge in 1684 to ask about planetary orbits under an inverse-square force.
Isaac Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica was published in 1687.
The Principia set out Isaac Newton's laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation.
Edmond Halley paid for the printing of the Principia because the Royal Society had spent its funds on De Historia Piscium.

key_moments.title: From professor to master of the Mint
key_moments.text: Newton left Cambridge to become **Warden of the Royal Mint** in 1696, during the **Great Recoinage**, and was made **Master of the Mint** in 1699, a post he held for the rest of his life. He took on the hunt for counterfeiters himself, gathering evidence and questioning witnesses, and his case against the forger **William Chaloner** ended with Chaloner hanged in 1699. In 1705 **Queen Anne** knighted him at Cambridge, an honour historians link more to an election campaign than to his science.
claims: Isaac Newton became Warden of the Royal Mint in 1696.
Isaac Newton became Master of the Royal Mint in 1699 and held the post until his death.
The counterfeiter William Chaloner was hanged in 1699 after being prosecuted by Isaac Newton.
Queen Anne knighted Isaac Newton in 1705, probably for political reasons connected with a parliamentary election.

deep_facts.text: The man often held up as the model of cold scientific reason spent years on **alchemy** and on reading the Bible for hidden prophecies, and wrote more on these subjects than on physics. The scale of it became clear only after his papers were sold at auction in 1936 and the economist **John Maynard Keynes** bought a large share of the alchemical manuscripts. Keynes read them and concluded that Newton was not the first of the age of reason but **the last of the magicians**.
claims: Isaac Newton wrote extensively on alchemy and biblical prophecy.
Many of Isaac Newton's unpublished papers were sold at a Sotheby's auction in 1936.
John Maynard Keynes bought many of Isaac Newton's alchemical manuscripts.
John Maynard Keynes described Isaac Newton as the last of the magicians rather than the first of the age of reason.

deep_facts.text: To find out whether colour came from the eye or from the light, Newton experimented on himself. His notebook records that he slid a **bodkin**, a blunt needle, between his eyeball and the bone of the eye socket and pressed until he saw **white, dark and coloured circles**. He also stared at the Sun in a mirror for so long that he reportedly had to stay in a dark room for days before his sight recovered.
claims: Isaac Newton recorded inserting a bodkin between his eye and the bone of the eye socket to study vision.
Isaac Newton reported seeing coloured circles when pressing on his eye with the bodkin.
Isaac Newton reportedly damaged his sight temporarily by looking at the Sun's reflection in a mirror.

deep_facts.text: One of Newton's longest-lasting legacies has nothing to do with physics. In 1717, as Master of the Mint, he set the value of the gold **guinea at 21 shillings**. Because this priced gold high compared with silver, silver coins drained out of circulation and Britain drifted, without any law being passed, onto a de facto **gold standard** that lasted until the twentieth century.
claims: In 1717 Isaac Newton, as Master of the Mint, set the value of the guinea at 21 shillings.
The 1717 valuation of the guinea overvalued gold compared with silver.
The 1717 guinea valuation helped move Britain onto a de facto gold standard.

connections.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
connections.connection: Developed calculus independently, sparking a bitter priority dispute in which a Royal Society report of 1712 sided with Newton.

connections.name: Edmond Halley
connections.connection: Prompted Newton to write the Principia after a 1684 visit and paid for its printing.

connections.name: Robert Hooke
connections.connection: Rival who attacked Newton's 1672 theory of light and later claimed credit for the inverse-square law.

connections.name: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica
connections.connection: Newton's 1687 book setting out the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

connections.name: Scientific Revolution
connections.connection: Newton's Principia is often treated as the culmination of this transformation of science.

connections.name: Johannes Kepler
connections.connection: Newton showed that Kepler's laws of planetary motion follow from an inverse-square law of gravity.

connections.name: Anne, Queen of Great Britain
connections.connection: Knighted Newton at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1705.

connections.name: John Maynard Keynes
connections.connection: Bought many of Newton's alchemical papers in 1936 and called him the last of the magicians.

connections.name: Voltaire
connections.connection: Popularised Newton's ideas in France and helped spread the apple story.
